title: Maternal epilepsy, prenatal antiseizure medication exposure, and risk of special education needs: A population-based cohort study in Wales
content:
by Alexia Karain, Jill P. Pell, Daniel F. Mackay, Scott Nelson, Sarjit Singh, Neha Rao, Michael Fleming

Background

Prenatal exposure to antiseizure medications (ASM) has been associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in children, although the contribution of maternal epilepsy itself remains unclear. This study aims to investigate associations between maternal epilepsy, prenatal ASM exposure and subsequent neurodevelopmental and educational outcomes.

Methods

A Welsh cohort was constructed of children born in 2009–2016 using linkage of routinely collected data in SAIL. Healthcare records identified children with prenatal exposure to at least one ASM and/or maternal epilepsy, with subgroup analyses by British National Formulary (BNF) ASM category and by individual ASM. Generalised estimating equations and Cox proportional hazard models were applied to a range of outcomes ascertained through linkage to school census and primary care records up to 13 years of age: special education needs (SEN), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), sensory impairments, communication problems, learning difficulties, physical/medical difficulties, emotional difficulties, and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Findings

Of the 179,024 liveborn children, 1,725 (~1.0%) were exposed to maternal epilepsy and/or ASMs in utero. All-cause SEN had non-specific associations with untreated (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.21–2.05) as well as treated (OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.38–1.92) maternal epilepsy, and all three BNF ASM categories; as did learning difficulties, communication and emotional problems. ADHD was associated with maternal epilepsy (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.06–2.11) but not prenatal ASM exposure. ASD was associated with prenatal exposure to sodium valproate (OR 3.07, 95% CI 1.16–8.15).

Conclusions

Associations with all-cause SEN, learning difficulties, communication and emotional problems, and ADHD were observed in relation to both treated and untreated maternal epilepsy, suggesting these associations may reflect maternal epilepsy and confounding by severity, with limited evidence supporting ASM-specific associations. The association between sodium valproate and ASD, although imprecise, is consistent with existing regulatory guidance restricting valproate use in pregnancy.
